title: Mahakassapa comes
hookLine: the great ascetic comes to him (Buddhacarita 17)

cards: Two robes on a roadside. One is a patched outer robe, but soft, folded into a seat under a tree. The other is rough hemp, worn thin, stitched together from rags.
In a little while, the two men wearing them will swap. The man with the soft robe is a seeker who has already left a wealthy home. The man with the rags is the Buddha.
This is how the discourses remember the meeting with Kassapa, later called Mahakassapa, great Kassapa. And the poem, in its seventeenth canto, sends him walking toward the Buddha too.

teach.b: First, what he left. Tradition remembers Kassapa as born into a wealthy brahmin family, and leaving it all, house, riches, a wife, to go looking for freedom.
Later tradition adds a tender detail: his wife, Bhadda, wanted the same thing, and the two of them went forth together, parting at a crossroads to walk different roads. Second, the meeting.
In his own words in the discourses, Kassapa says he saw the Buddha sitting by a shrine on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, and knew at once: this is my teacher.
He bowed and said so, and the Buddha taught him there by the road. Third, the robes.

teach.h: A SOFT CLOAK FOR A RAG-ROBE.
teach.b: Kassapa folded his cloak for the Buddha to sit on. The Buddha remarked how soft it was. Kassapa offered it, and the Buddha gave him his own worn rag-robe in return.
It's a small, strange exchange, and some readers take it as a sign: the teacher handing his robe to someone who would carry the teaching on. Fourth, what he became.
The discourses list Kassapa as foremost among the monks who kept the strict ascetic practices: living in the forest, eating only alms food, wearing rag-robes.
He came after the first five, after Yasas and the fire-keepers. He wasn't the first.
But in the stories, he became one of the great ones, and tradition says that after the Buddha's death it was Kassapa who called the monks together to remember what had been taught.
The great ones don't all arrive at the start.

how: Mahakassapa is honored in Theravada as a model of forest and ascetic practice, and in Zen lineages as the first heir of the teaching after the Buddha. Monks in forest traditions still keep some of the strict practices he is remembered for.

games.q: you're Kassapa. you've folded your good cloak for the teacher to sit on, and he says how soft it is. what do you do?
games.why: Kassapa offers it, and the Buddha gives him his own worn rag-robe in return.

practice: Bring to mind someone who joined something after you did, a family, a team, a circle of friends, and who may never have felt part of the founding story.
Notice one thing they carry now that no one else does, and rest with the breath, holding them in that light.

wordCard.voice: Mahakassapa comes. A wealthy brahmin who left home, met the Buddha by a roadside shrine, and traded his soft cloak for a rag-robe. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the great ones arrive. Coming late made him no less great. That's day seven hundred twenty.
